title: Sliding window patterns
body: Sliding window solves problems over contiguous subarrays or substrings by maintaining a range and updating it as its boundaries move. For a fixed-size window, add the new right value and remove the value leaving on the left. This reduces repeated work from O(nk) to O(n). Variable-size windows expand and shrink to maintain a condition. Common prompts ask for the longest or shortest contiguous span meeting a constraint.

title: Two pointers
body: Two pointers track two positions in a sequence and move them based on a condition. Opposite-direction pointers are useful on sorted arrays for pair sums and palindrome checks. Same-direction pointers can build or partition a range. State the invariant, explain why a move cannot skip a valid answer, and analyze the total number of pointer moves. Typical complexity is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

title: Complexity analysis
body: Big O describes how resource use grows with input size. Count dominant operations and simplify constants and lower-order terms. Sequential loops add their costs; nested loops often multiply them. Account for auxiliary space separately from input storage. For recursive algorithms, write a recurrence and identify recursion depth and per-call work.

title: Binary search on answer
body: Binary search on answer applies when feasibility is monotonic: if a candidate value works, all values on one side also work. Define a predicate feasible(x), choose bounds that contain the answer, and maintain a clear invariant about which half still contains it. Use overflow-safe midpoint arithmetic in fixed-width languages and prove termination. Complexity is O(log range) times the cost of one feasibility check.

title: Dynamic programming foundations
body: Dynamic programming fits problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Define a state that captures everything future decisions need, write the recurrence, identify base cases, and choose an evaluation order. Memoization follows recursive dependencies; tabulation fills states iteratively. Reduce memory only after confirming which previous states are required.

title: SOLID design principles
body: SOLID is a set of object-oriented design principles: single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, and dependency inversion. Apply them to reduce coupling and make behavior easier to extend or test. They are guidelines rather than a checklist; explain the concrete change in responsibilities or dependencies and avoid introducing abstractions without a real variation point.

title: Choosing a design pattern
body: Choose a design pattern to address a specific change or collaboration problem. Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms; Observer distributes state changes; Factory centralizes object creation; State models behavior that varies by lifecycle state. Start from requirements and likely changes, define class responsibilities, then introduce the smallest pattern that clarifies the design.

title: Capacity estimation
body: Estimate system scale with explicit assumptions. Convert daily active users and actions per user into requests per second, distinguish average from peak traffic, and estimate storage growth from writes, retention, and replication. Round estimates to useful orders of magnitude and use them to guide decisions such as caching, partitioning, and asynchronous processing.

title: Reliability and failure handling
body: Design for partial failures. Set timeouts, bound retries with backoff and jitter, make operations idempotent where possible, and isolate overloaded dependencies with queues or circuit breakers. Discuss consistency and availability needs per operation, define service-level objectives, and identify how failures are observed and recovered.

title: Retrieval augmented generation
body: RAG retrieves relevant source chunks and supplies them to a language model at answer time. A basic pipeline ingests documents, splits them into meaningful chunks, stores embeddings with metadata, retrieves candidates for a query, optionally reranks them, and generates a grounded response with citations. Evaluate retrieval recall separately from answer faithfulness. Apply access filters before content reaches the model.

title: Evaluating LLM applications
body: Evaluate the system at multiple layers: retrieval relevance, answer correctness, groundedness, refusal behavior, latency, and cost. Build a representative dataset with expected answers and edge cases, use deterministic checks where possible, and calibrate model-based graders against human review. Run regression evaluations whenever prompts, models, or content change.

title: Agent workflows and tool use
body: Use an agent workflow when a task needs explicit steps, branching, tools, retries, or resumable state. Keep each node focused, validate tool inputs, apply least privilege, and set step and time limits. Prefer a predictable graph for known workflows; allow model-driven routing only where it adds value. Trace node inputs and outputs and evaluate complete runs, not only final text.
